fixtures.intent: The base lawful obligation: memo mode, sequence allocation, comfortable margins.
Tagged redemption mode carries an exact DestinationTag and a distinct commitment.
A pre-created Ticket carries the transaction instead of the account sequence.
Generation 1 is authorized once generation 0 is proven not successful.
A one-drop obligation still converts exactly and authorizes.
A required tag of zero is distinct from no tag and must still authorize.
An unsupported schema version fails closed rather than being interpreted.
A binding for a different asset manager is a cross-domain replay.
A retired binding may not authorize anything.
Only an ACTIVE obligation can be paid.
An obligation assigned to another agent is not ours to pay.
One obligation can produce at most one validated successful payment.
Re-signing the same generation is a replay.
Both the block and the time limit have passed, so the obligation can no longer be paid.
LastLedgerSequence leaves too few ledgers before the obligation's last block.
The projected close time leaves too little time before the obligation's deadline.
A LastLedgerSequence at or behind the validated ledger can never be included.
A destination that is not a canonical classic address is never repaired.
A single-character corruption breaks base58check and must be rejected.
Paying the bound account itself is never a lawful redemption payment.
A fee that consumes the whole value leaves nothing lawful to pay.
A UBA amount that is not a whole number of drops must refuse, never round.
A reference for a different request id can never close this obligation.
A well-formed reference of the wrong FAssets type is still invalid.
XRPL destination tags are 32-bit; a wider value cannot be represented.
A tag value on an untagged obligation is a field the agent must not add.
A fee spike above the configured ceiling is refused, not absorbed.
Reusing a sequence an earlier generation holds risks two validated payments.
The same collision rule applies to Tickets.
A revoked extension version may not produce an accepted result.
Running code the binding never approved is a stale or substituted version.
A result from another registered extension is out of domain.
Emergency pause stops new authorizations.
A paused agent cannot receive a new authorization.
Unavailable state is transient and must not be recorded as a policy denial.
No binding means nothing to authorize against.
The central replacement rule: never replace while the earlier attempt is unresolved.
A later generation with no record of the earlier one cannot be justified.
A key mid-rotation must not sign.
An emergency-revoked key must not sign.
A malformed bound source account is a configuration failure that fails closed.
An action carrying another Flare chain id is a cross-domain replay (I-011).
A well-formed instruction sender that is not the bound one is still foreign (I-011).
An action for another XRPL network would produce a payment on the wrong ledger.
A zero-value obligation has nothing lawful to pay, independent of the fee.
A multi-signed transaction costs base fee times one plus signatures; underpaying never validates (I-007).
The same signer list authorizes once the fee meets the multi-sign floor exactly.
Under FDC proof latency FAssets can still report ACTIVE while XRPL already paid; a second signature would be a duplicate (I-009).
An unresolved earlier attempt blocks replacement even after the window has expired, and the reason must stay the replacement one (I-010, ADR 0002 ordering).
A fee exactly at the cap is lawful; the check is a ceiling, not a strict bound.
One drop past the cap refuses, pinning the inequality direction.
LastLedgerSequence exactly at the ledger-margin limit is lawful; the time margin is given ample headroom so this isolates the ledger inequality.
One ledger past the margin limit refuses, pinning the inequality direction.
The largest representable XRPL destination tag is lawful.

At equality the obligation is not yet expired, but no lawful LastLedgerSequence remains: it would have to exceed the validated ledger and not exceed the last underlying block at once. The refusal must be the margin one, not the expiry one.
One past both limits is genuinely expired, and the reason changes to the expiry one.
The largest uint64 request id still derives a valid payment reference.
A history missing generation 1 means the caller lost track of the obligation; a decision built on it would be guesswork.
A duplicated generation in the history is an inconsistent record, not a resolved one.
A history shorter than the generation number is the omission a lying coordinator would attempt (I-009).
An older unresolved attempt must not be buried under a newer resolved one; every generation is checked, not just the last (I-010).
A negative generation is rejected by policy, not left to fail deep inside the encoder.
the agent had already paid this obligation and the observation saw it, which is the case that produced a real duplicate payment on Coston2 before V2 existed
a payment carrying this obligation's reference for the wrong amount still refuses; a near miss is a state for a human, not a state to pay over the top of
a payment to the same destination carrying a different obligation's reference is not this obligation and must not block it
a provisional payment is not a result, so it does not count as already paid; only a validated one does
a decision that did not look at the ledger must not be indistinguishable from one that looked and saw nothing
the observation could not be completed, which is transient and must never authorize
independently operated endpoints contradicted each other about whether this obligation is already paid
one endpoint is one party; the policy requires independent agreement before an observation counts
an observation older than the policy allows is refused, because the ledger has moved on since
an observation of a ledger the caller has not seen validated is incoherent, and an incoherent observation is a fabricated one
a V1 input cannot carry the observation V2 requires, so accepting it would be accepting exactly the blindness that caused the incident
a malformed observed transaction hash must fail closed in both languages. Go was silently substituting 32 zero bytes and signing; the reference model threw and refused.
two observed payments sharing a transaction hash must produce one root in both languages. Go's sort is not stable and JavaScript's is, so ordering by hash alone gave two different commitments.
the same two payments supplied in the opposite order must give the identical commitment, which is what a total order buys and a stable-sort-by-hash does not.
